maintopic: POSSIBLE MACKENZIE VALLEY PIPELINE-USE OF CANADIAN LABOUR, EQUIPMENT AND MATERIALS-DISCUSSIONS WITH SASKATCHEWAN AND ALBERTA
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I think the guidelines issued last August, which represent the government's position in respect of a pipeline, were very clear in this respect. Guideline number one, I believe, indicates there will be a clear preference for maximum Canadian content in any application that is made in respect of the construction of a pipeline.

maintopic: POSSIBLE MACKENZIE VALLEY PIPELINE-USE OF CANADIAN LABOUR, EQUIPMENT AND MATERIALS-DISCUSSIONS WITH SASKATCHEWAN AND ALBERTA
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, is the minister in a position to advise us whether there have been any discussions with the governments of Alberta and Saskatchewan in reference to their position regarding such a pipeline which will go through their territory, and have there been any guarantees given to these two provincial governments that producers of natural gas and crude petroleum in those provinces will get a share of the oil flow going to the United States or elsewhere in Canada?

speakerposition: Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
maintopic: POSSIBLE MACKENZIE VALLEY PIPELINE-USE OF CANADIAN LABOUR, EQUIPMENT AND MATERIALS-DISCUSSIONS WITH SASKATCHEWAN AND ALBERTA
speechtext: There have been discussions of a general nature with the governments of both Alberta and Saskatchewan but not in respect of the specifics of a proposed pipeline. Until there is an application we cannot indicate to the provinces exactly what might be their interests and what might be the resolution in respect of their property rights.

maintopic: POSSIBLE MACKENZIE VALLEY PIPELINE-USE OF CANADIAN LABOUR, EQUIPMENT AND MATERIALS-DISCUSSIONS WITH SASKATCHEWAN AND ALBERTA
speechtext: In view of the fact that the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development has said to the United States that the government would likely entertain such an application for the construction of a pipeline by the United States, does the minister not consider that, because of the jurisdiction of the two Prairie provinces I mentioned, some form of discussion should be had now with them before any further suggestion is made to or negotiations carried on with the United States? I ask this question in view of the fact that this proposed pipeline will go through the territory of the two Prairie provinces.

speakerposition: Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
maintopic: POSSIBLE MACKENZIE VALLEY PIPELINE-USE OF CANADIAN LABOUR, EQUIPMENT AND MATERIALS-DISCUSSIONS WITH SASKATCHEWAN AND ALBERTA
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, in the normal course when there is an application in respect of the building of a pipeline the provinces are represented at the hearing before the National Energy Board. They make their cases very clearly and their viewpoints are always considered. It may well be that in a matter of this national importance, and because of the fact this will be such a tremendous economic undertaking to the benefit of Canada, if it goes ahead, there should be earlier discussion. We are certainly prepared to consider that at the appropriate time.

Mr. Speaker, some time ago the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources said that an application for the construction of such a pipeline would be considered by the National Energy Board and that it has the responsibility for ensuring the safety of the ecology. I should like to ask the minister whether the National Energy Board has carried out ecological studies and has the necessary staff to do so, or whether it will use the surveys which have been made by the Department of Indian Affairs and Northern Development?

speakeroldname: Hon. J. J. Greene (Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources):
speakerposition: Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, there is a very clear emphasis placed on the ecological safety of such a line. The National Energy Board has very competent engineers who consider these questions on a continuing basis. The private sector, both at Normal Wells in respect of a gas line and at Inuvik in respect of an oil line, are doing very comprehensive research. The Department of Indian Affairs and Northern Development has a very clear responsibility, which it has undertaken, as enunciated again by the guidelines of last August. That department is responsible for the area in the territories, and the entire federal government responsibility in respect of ecology is being correlated by an interdepartmental committee on the ecological safety of pipelines in the north.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order. Hon. members will notice that there are at least four hon. members seeking the opportunity to ask supplementary questions on this matter. Very shortly we will be running out of time, and I wonder whether we should spend another five or ten minutes on this important subject. For the moment the Chair will recognize the hon. member for Nanaimo-Cowichan-The Islands.

Mr. Speaker, in view of the fact that the National Energy Board Act deals mainly with safety and makes no reference to the protection of the ecology, although a broad interpretation could be placed on the words "safety and public interest", can the minister assure the House that all the research which has been carried out and will continue to be done in respect of the ecology of the north will be placed before the National Energy Board when this application is heard, in the event that such an application is made?

speakerposition: Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in the first instance I believe that in accord with the guidelines the ecological question will have to be considered and approved by the Department of Indian Affairs and Northern Development. That department has the primary ecological responsibility. The evidence of the department's findings and its views would then be placed before the board. As my hon. friend has pointed out, the actual wording of the National Energy Board Act refers to safety and the public interest. It may well be a valid suggestion that the Act



should be amended to make specific reference to pollution and ecology.

speechtext: Order, please. I regret to interrupt, but the hon. member for South Western Nova is rising on a point of order.

speechtext: I do not quarrel with the point made by the hon. member, but there still has to be some limitation. Hon. members will realize that the discretion is left in the hands of the Speaker. Mr. Speaker, I have a question for the Minister of Regional Economic Expansion.
I would like to ask him whether he is aware of a resolution of the municipal council of the city of Mont-magny mentioning the intense unemployment situation in Montmagny and the neighbouring region and asking that Montmagny and its suburbs be designated as special zones, or else be included in a new development program to be set up as early as possible.
I would also ask the minister whether he has taken action on this request. If so, could he tell the House what steps will be taken to cope effectively with this request which, in my opinion, is quite justified?

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, Montmagny is included in a

designated area, which means that industries wishing to locate there are entitled to subsidies from my department. In spite of that, not many new industries have settled in that locality. I do not think that the fact of making Montmagny a special area would greatly alter the situation.

Would the Minister of Regional Economic Expansion tell us if he has received such a request from the authorities of the town of Montmagny?
Mr. Speaker, I recall having read a resolution from the council of the Town of Montmagny. I would have to read it again to be sure if such a request was contained in the resolution.

The House resumed, from Thursday, March 4, consideration of the motion of Mr. Benson that Bill C-225, to amend the Income Tax Act and to amend an act to amend that act, be read the second time and referred to a Committee of the Whole.

Mr. Speaker, last Thursday, the House dealt with the amendments we proposed to Bill C-225.
It worries me to see so many members leave the House at this moment because this is an important bill since it seeks to tax Canadians for one more year.
The explanatory notes to clause 2 of Bill C-225 read as follows:
This amendment would extend for one year the temporary surtaxes imposed under Part IA of the Income Tax Act.
The surtax on an individual is 3 per cent of his "basic tax" in excess of $200. It would be extended to apply to the 1971 taxation year.
And it is also stated:
The surtax on a corporation is 3 per cent of its tax computed under section 39 or 69 of the Income Tax Act. It would be extended to apply to profits earned in 1971.
The specific and only purpose of this bill is to extend this tax for another year, namely, to April 1, 1972.
I should have liked, Mr. Speaker, to commend the Minister of Finance (Mr. Benson), but as the economic
situation in Canada, for which he does not bear the whole responsibility, but the major part of it is very bad, particularly with regard to unemployment, more especially in Quebec. I find that instead of praising him I must tell him that he and his government have failed in attempting to find solutions to the economic problems of Canada.
Mr. Speaker, we are members of the sovereign Parliament of our country which has all the authority required to eliminate any anti-human conditions created by man. This is not a municipal council with no authority to legislate in financial matters. This is the sovereign Parliament which is all-powerful in the field of finance. It is not in a sovereign Parliament such as ours that financial limitations must be discussed. The financial resources of a country may be limited only by its economic resources. If there are financial limitations in a country of unlimited resources such as ours, it is only because there are financial limitations due to the ignorance of those whose responsibility it is to govern the country. The difficulty lies within human brains which are conditioned by ignorance and finance, or are contaminated by them.
Mr. Speaker, the financiers' intellectual constipation is at the basis of all our economic problems.
Recently, the hon. member for Frontenac (Mr. Cor-riveau), in the only speech he has made in this House since he was elected, taught us a new expression in the economic field. He said that there was a "capitalism of the mind", but he did not explain what was this "capitalism of the mind". I never saw, in any book of political economy, the explanation for "capitalism of the mind".
The hon. member said also that it was necessary to increase our production in order to solve our problems. He should go and say that to the Frontenac farmers, who are presently penalized because they have produced or are still producing too much milk. He should say that to the farmers of western Canada who are in the same position. And immediately afterwards he said we should produce more and sell our surpluses.
Finally he said that there was a puzzle to solve.
Mr. Speaker, if there is a puzzle, it is not where the hon. member for Frontenac and many others think it is, but it is in his imagination, in his head.
You may recall however that the government did and promised everything in order to get that champion of the "capitalism of the mind" elected.
"It should sit at the negotiation table", he told us. What kind of negotiations? Where are their results?
Once more the expectations of the people of Frontenac have been disappointed. The election campaign in the riding is now over, and so are the wild utterances. Let us now look at the only results, which are negative at all levels of the national economy.
Last year, I often happened to listen to a popular program on the Hull radio, which invariably began by the same words: "The world is sick". The speaker, through this remark, unfortunately was reflecting the economic climate in which we live, which the present Minister of Finance (Mr. Benson) complacently enforces on the Canadian people.

Since 1968, we have been witnessing the government's political and economic somersaults and we must recognize that the government, and particularly the Minister of Finance, that financial quack, who is not in the House this afternoon, have no remedy to offer which is likely to solve the country's economic problems and bring Canada back to the prosperity it formerly experienced, so that the people could also live again, because Canadians are still prepared to make the necessary efforts to bring economic prosperity to Canada.
As reported in Hansard of December 3, 1970, on page 1743, the Minister of Finance said, and I quote:
-I have no new general tax measures to propose tonight-
That sums up the speech made by the Minister of Finance and this government fiscal policy: "No tax measures to propose". That means we shall continue to suffer our ills and have the same troubles that we have had for the last several years. We shall continue to be economically ill.
This means also that we shall continue to walk blindly, to retreat, to go round in a circle, progressing towards a just society for some, as we have known it, especially in the last few years.
The people, a large proportion of which is unfortunately too easily misled by the government's well-organized propaganda, continue to believe in the financial quackery of the Minister of Finance.
A quack, Mr. Speaker, is a man who is always trying something new and who, when a patient consults him says: Take these white pills; we shall see what happens. When they do not produce the expected result, he will say: Take these pink pills. They contain the same ingredients, only the colour is different. The pink pills having failed, he will be given a new green liquid: Try that, then come and see me again. The quack thus continues his experiments, exploiting the patient who hopes to be cured.
These past 100 years, financial quacks have given us similar results. Who can tell the difference between the liberal taxes and the progressive conservative taxes, between the liberal debts and the progressive conservative debts that have been inflicted upon us for 100 years? What is the difference between "red" and "blue" taxes or between the liberal tax to which we are going to object but which, unfortunately, the government will still pass?
What difference is there between "red" and "blue" crises? Between "red" and "blue" bankruptcies? Between "red and "blue" rationing? Between "red" and "blue" inflation? Between "red" and "blue" misery? Between "red" and "blue" bureaucracy? Between "red and blue" unemployment?
Mr. Speaker, I could keep on indefinitely with the list of these economic ailments under the present system treated by the quack doctors of finance who are interested in keeping Canada and Canadians economically ill, so as to carry on with their practice of financial quackery.

I keep on repeating this word, because it is very important. The minister acts like a quack or like an amateur mechanic. Mr. Speaker, the Minister of Finance is getting ready to stifle the Canadian people economically.
What I find most shocking is how the government can, on the one hand, show such ability, through the Minister of Finance, in stifling private enterprise and, on the other hand, thanks to its well planned publicity-and Information Canada will soon confirm this-convince the Canadian people that they are being stifled for their own good.
Unemployment and bankruptcies are the symptoms of an ill-planned economy. The FLQ, in Quebec or elsewhere, is another economic symptom. The millions of people on welfare are yet another economic symptom. The widespread dissent as well as the strikes are as many economic symptoms. And if the Minister of Finance is unable to root out the causes of all our economic ills, either he is a quack or he is party to our economic system which keeps the country and its people in a state of economic illness.
As for me, Mr. Speaker, I believe the Minister of Finance is more a quack than an accomplice. And I feel only pity for the poor Canadian people who will have to pay, in 1971, more than $2 billion in interests on the national public debt, because of a Minister of Finance who does nothing but deprive the people in order to make finance thrive all the more.

Mr. Speaker, I have in hand a copy of Bill C-225 entitled: An act to amend the Income Tax Act and to amend an Act to amend that Act.
The title itself is ambiguous. No doubt this is due to the confusion that existed in Parliament in 1968, when the Liberal partisans, caught off their guard, had to make important concessions to taxpayers and refund overpayments under a legislation which had not yet been passed.
What a contrast between the slowness of the government to seek answers to unemployment and other problems and its undue haste to carry out regulations establishing the right to tax. They are the ones who accuse the members of the Ralliement creditiste of delaying the proceedings of the House. Yet taxpayers are in no hurry to be taxed, either under an amending bill or another legislation such as Bill C-225 now under consideration or any other money-pumping method to get at the generally insufficient income of Canadians.
The moment income tax is mentioned, very few citizens are enthusiastic, except the lackeys of the financial system who do not seem to realize all the problems they are creating for Canadian workers with their taxing gimmick that takes the most different forms they are forced to imagine because of the stupid system they try to defend.
For a long time, various categories of workers, particularly forest workers and others, have been trying to make the Minister of Finance (Mr. Benson) understand that travelling expenses incurred in their search for a job, the purchase of costly tools such as power saws and others should be deductible under the Income Tax Act. No improvement is coming in that regard.
It is only after 20 years of making representations that Canadian workers who were helping red or blue governments ease the unemployment problem by going to work for the forest industry in the United States, particularly in Maine and New Hampshire, that authorities on both sides of the border understood that they should allow those workers to get unemployment benefits when they were out of work. The "tax pumping" system begins to work from the very first working days. In order to please the tax-happy people in the United States Canada and Quebec, the worker who has to work hard to earn a living must file three income tax returns, with all the complications involved. It is therefore easy to understand why the workers revolt at times.
We are living in a period when laws and regulations are being extended for the purpose of maintaining a taxing right, which at the outset was to last only a year. We must therefore condemn such extended taxes. Even though the supporters of such a system do not like to be reminded of the ill effects of their laws and regulations, they must recognize that only indebtedness is making some progress.
I have here an article from the March 9, 1971 edition of La Presse, bearing the title: Canadian indebtedness increases. Canada's Minister of Finance keeps on sailing through those stormy circumstances, tossed about by the elements of an artificial financial system, that is creating taxes, debts, unpaid and unpayable, under the present system. By means of the surprising acrobatic stunts he resorts to at times, he succeeds in maintaining the dollar in a floating position.
It is the last straw.

His rather eccentric behaviour reminds us of the recent enough story of a ship that sailed for some time at random, and was sold later for less than the cost of repairs and painting. Let us hope that the ship of state will succeed in overcoming the imaginary waves of inflation and that it will finally reach a port



where competent engineers will be able to perform the necessary repairs to its rudder.
If we look at the way the government is spending the money which it succeeds in taking from the taxpayers thanks to disguised taxes of all kinds, we quickly agree with the Auditor General about the administrators' blunders.
I have with me an editorial of the CJMS broadcasting station of February 20, 1971, which shows that the taxes paid by the Canadian taxpayers are not always properly used. And I quote:
-In the same week, two facts have come to our attention. Further inquiry might multiply them by ten, twenty and even more. Let us take the case of adult education. Everybody knows that for retraining purposes, a person can be paid $35 to $80 per week depending on family conditions provided he is attending adult training courses. However, do you know that, in Montreal, a part-time teacher is teaching on the Canadian novel to permit workmen aged 20 to 35 and more to obtain the credits they need to complete grade 9 while his own education stopped at grade 8? This teacher is paid $25 per night for a 2-hour course and the others are paid, as we said, to attend such courses which will be useless to them when they get back on the labour market. This is incredible nonsense which shows the lack of seriousness of those responsible for the programming of these courses. And this is done with our money, with taxpayers' money. Another case-
Since he came to Montreal, a German immigrant has first attended French lessons. He was paid to attend. Once the French course was over, he registered for English lessons. Again he is getting paid. When he has acquired a knowledge of English and French, it is possible that he will immigrate this time to the United States, after having lived here two years at the expense of the Canadian taxpayers. All this is not serious. I am prepared to get the publication put out by the federal government and entitled: "How your tax dollar is spent". I am eager to know whether such facts are recorded in that publication. To you, to me, taxpayers, rotating teachers' strikes are costing $50 million. And what about the postal strike? Taxpayers are fed up and rightly so.
The supporters of the Ralliement Creditiste positively state that the purchasing power which is in the hands of Canadian consumers is inadequate to buy Canadian production, taking into account prevailing prices. It is not by taxing them that the problem will be solved.
Although there are many causes to that state of affairs, it is possible to demonstrate easily the validity of that statement.
The banking system is the source of all the Canadian money which is issued in the form of loans. However, the banking system lends money on the sole condition that a larger amount-capital and interest-than that which has been loaned will be paid back. Therefore, when a producer borrows to finance his production, if he is to remain in business, he must include that charge in prices when he sells his product. But since the equivalent of that additional amount has not at any time been distributed as purchasing power to the consumer, it is obvious that the consumer is unable to pay the prices charged by the producer for his products.

In his book entitled Distribution of Production, Major Douglas states:
Banks can create money in five minutes and this is what they have been doing for centuries.
On the other hand, Mr. Reginald McKenna, of Great Britain, at the annual meeting of the Midland Bank, on January 25, 1924, had this to say, and I quote:
The amount of money in existence varies only through the action of the banks, as they increase or decrease the deposits. Any bank loan destroys a deposit.
Banks can create and destroy money and bank credit amounts to money. It is with the help of that money that most transactions are being performed and not through what we usually call dollars.
Moreover, I am in agreement with the remarks that Mr. Hawtrey, under-secretary of the treasury in Great Britain, over the B.B.C. network, in London, on March 22, 1933; he asserted his agreement with Major Douglas explicitly:
Moreover, I agree with him (C. H. Douglas) when he says that the banks create money and economic crises are created by the banking system.
When a bank makes a loan, it creates money out of nothing.
In his book The Art of Central Banking, the author also says:
When a bank provides a loan, it creates credit. While a loan is being shown as a credit in its books, an equal amount is being registered as a liability.
Finally, Lord Keynes, economist, and during the last world war, governor of the Bank of England, had this to say:
There is no doubt that all bank deposits are created by the banks.
In conclusion, may I quote from the evidence Mr. Graham Towers, governor of the Bank of Canada, gave before the committee on banking and commerce in Ottawa, in 1939:
Each time a bank provides a loan or buys securities, new banking credit is created-new deposits-truly new money. Generally speaking, all new money is created by the banks under the guise of loans.
In 1965, Mr. Paul A. Samuelson, internationally famous economist, in a book that was translated into French under the title L'economique: techniques modernes de I'analyse economique, explained how the banks provided an irrefutable answer to the question: Where does the money come from?
Unfortunately, Mr. Speaker, the phenomenon is not too well understood. Most people have heard that, thanks to some sleight-of-hand trick, banks are able to make money out of nothing. Few people, however, realize how that is done. In this regard, I will quote from page 277 of Samuelson's book:
In fact, there is nothing magic or unintelligible about bank deposits. Any intelligent person can follow step by step what happens to bank accounts. The real explanation of the creation of deposits is a simple one. The only difficulty is to understand the false versions which continue to abound.

They would surely be only too happy to be able to do this. But they know better than anybody else that no banker can invest funds which are not at his disposal-and any money used to purchase securities or to grant a loan must immediately leave his bank.
This is why bankers often go to the other extreme.

They readily maintain that on the whole, the banking system is also unable to coin money. "After all, they say, we can only invest the funds left to us by our customers. We do not create them. We only put the community savings at work." Now, the bankers who put forward this argument are completely mistaken. They have been snared by an old acquaintance of ours, the rhetorical sophism-but we must not forget that what is true for each of us is not necessarily true for all. The banking system on the whole can accomplish what a single bank is unable to do.
We there answer in the affirmative to the question which heads the present section:
CAN BANKS REALLY CREATE MONEY?
Yes, the American banking system and the American public jointly create approximately $5 worth of bank deposits for each dollar taken out of circulation and handed over to the banks.
In the same book, in order to back up his statement, the economist uses four tables starting with the first bank stage and tracing the chain reactions of a $1,000 deposit on the other banks.
This explanation may be understood by all those who are willing to go to the trouble of studying the system thoroughly.
Let us recall the following words of the wisest of statesmen, Abraham Lincoln:
The privilege to create and issue money is not only the sovereign prerogative of a government, it is also the greatest creative power.
Money must circulate for the sake of the country's development, just as if Canada were at war, and we are actually at war against internal foes, that is unemployment and hardship.
If this government really wanted to establish the just society that its leader promised the Canadian people during the 1968 election campaign, it could do so. A serious effort, a simple decision would be enough, and Canadians would be assured of a decent living, of freedom and security, because the two always go together. Our ancestors have fought for those two ideals in order to be able to pass them on to us. Even if the people enjoyed security from the cradle to the grave, as some socialist and communist leaders claim to be able to guarantee, in losing their freedom the people would also lose their soul. There is no happiness in security if one becomes a slave, if one loses one's right to choose.
On the other hand, what kind of happiness may we expect from this freedom of ours if we have lost our security? The one without the other serves no purpose. We can and we must enjoy freedom and security at the same time in a country such as Canada.
Let us consider the vast natural resources with which our country has been blessed by Providence. Let us consider the fertile lands from which we could draw more food than we need. Let us ask ourselves whether there is not enough of this plenty to provide economic security for our whole population for hundreds of years to come? What is preventing us enjoying it all? With more riches per capita than any other country, we should enjoy the highest standard of living in the whole world. Why is it not so? We, Creditistes, maintain without fear of being contradicted, that it is this deteriorated and outmoded financial system controlled by trusts, fostered and supported by stupid politicians, which prevents the nation from distributing the abundance that surrounds us.
To be truly consistent with man's natural aspirations, the real solution will have to be sought in an increased freedom for all individuals, and not in new limitations of the freedoms they have left. Such a solution would in no way be incompatible with the security that governments impose upon us on the grounds that it is the wish of the public. Citizens do demand a minimum of security, but they do not ask for a straight jacket. Security must be confortable and pleasant if we are to enjoy it fully. It must not stifle us and become execrable under the clumsy hands of its makers. Individuals can achieve it, if only governments would remove the obstacles that they themselves have put in the way, if only governments would consolidate the foundations of our economic structure instead of merely making occasional repairs. Sooner or later, the building will collapse. A chronic headache cannot be cured by taking tablets: the pain may be temporarily eased off, but its cause still remains.
Once the building has collapsed, the only thing left for our progeny will be to write our history and they will gaze with amazement at the unbelievable spectable that we will have supplied them with. If we were to be confronted with them, their opinion would shame us. They may write: "The people of the twentieth century had a strange behaviour! They were great masters in the art of producing goods and wealth but unsuccessful in distributing them. These same people, rather than increase figures, for fear of shortage preferred to restrict the production of goods. Their greatly advanced knowledge enabled them to reach the uninhabited moon while whole populations on their own planet remained inaccessible and destitute.
They feared production more than destruction: they restricted money deliberately in order to limit production, consumption and life. Money flowed profusely and without limits to stir up war and hasten demolition and death. They wasted with unspeakable lavishness the time of thousands of their fellow citizens as they condemned



them to unaccountable unemployment. They sowed broadcast, happily, remorseless, the precious time of other thousands of citizens, to dole out to these unemployed a relative security from savings previously forced upon them.
They asked for an acceleration of production in order to cut down prices, and they recommended decreasing consumption with for the same purpose. Out and out imports were considered a disaster, the source of all misfortunes for a nation: a citizen was neither virtuous nor patriotic if he consumed imported products. But strangely enough, the citizens as a whole would become patriotic and virtuous if they succeeded in imposing this calamity to another people through out and out exports. Their big mistake was failing to realize that time is the only wealth that can be lost irrevocably. All other riches can wait until man is ready to exploit them to his own profit.
All this is strange, bizarre, extraordinary! But nowadays just mentioning these self-evident truths is enough to be branded as a dreamer, to make other people shrug their shoulders.
Advocates of this theory will be asked to be realistic, they will be suspected of being a little off the beam, but no one will never try to prove them wrong. They will be given the chance to admit it freely, that is if someone takes the trouble to listen to them, but they will never venture on the field of evidence. Obviously, they are wrong and they are told that they do not think the same way as the masterminds of our century. And yet, the truth is so simple that it seems incredible: the time of man is the only resource needed to develop matter, and it is the only one which is unrecoverable once it is lost.
Taking into account the present situation in Canada, the government authorities should not take too long before deciding to establish the "just society" that all Canadians aspire to.
Mr: Leonel Beaudoin (Richmond): Mr. Speaker, no member of this House can offord to miss the opportunity of blaming openly the present government for its fiscal policy, as stated in the bill now under study, namely Bill C-225, entitled "An Act to amend the Income Tax Act and to amend an Act to amend that Act".
Last Wednesday night, March 3, I took part, with a few colleagues from the opposition, in a discussion with the management of the Canadian Labour Congress. We discussed with this organization, which represents a million workers or more, the implications of the brief they had submitted to the government of Canada last March 1.
I agree generally with what is included in this brief, and I fully endorse a paragraph on page 13 dealing directly with the bill we are presently studying, which reads:
It seems that a number of measures could be taken, most of them having a rather immediate stimulating effect on the economy in addition to bringing some relief to the people who need them. We should like to propose, for instance, an immediate personal income tax reduction in favour of lower income groups. Since those people have a strong tendency to spend any extra income or savings they might have, this would

And the same old story repeats itself today. Having reached that stage, why does the Minister of Finance (Mr. Benson) not seek a temporary extension-to use his own words-of that surtax, for an indefinite period? Thus, the population would not know where it stands with such a government and, at the next general elections, it would know what to do.
Mr. Speaker, in order to believe in those temporary extensions, one must really have divine confidence in our leaders, which I, unfortunately, do not have.
Not only do they continue to tax Canadians with such laws, but they also contribute to get us bogged down in a system which has already proved, and which is still proving every day how illogical it is.
I consider that taxes, as they are used in the present system, are to say the least a little dishonest because, in my opinion, they must exist only to withdraw the excess money in circulation, in the face of the obvious fact that there is a lack of consumer products. But are there really too many products? I do not believe so. Is there a surplus of money? Certainly not, at least as far as I am concerned, and I would be glad to know anyone who is in the opposite situation, except naturally the few politicians who continue to believe that there are such people.
Why not at last realize that it is not the taxes which maintain a healthy economy, but a system adequate to the needs of consumers. We all know that bills like the one before us have been introduced since the coming into existence of the system and that we shall have more of them as long as the system exists in its present form.
What would be the use of freeing the producer within the industry, if the whole economic system, including the producer and the consumer and therefore industry itself and its elements, remains under the yoke of banks, which seem to be the "parents" of the present system? The only thing to do in order to free the community would be for the State, brain of the social body, to administer the

banking system and oblige it to serve the people and not enslave them as it does, especially since we have been hearing about the just society from this government which I look upon as the most autocratic the Canadian people, have ever know.
Through this bill, we are laying for another year a new fiscal load on the taxpayers who have not enough money to get what would be necessary for a decent living, while there is an abundance of products in this country. Therefore I regard this extension of the 3 per cent surtax as pure and simple robbery or at least like something dishonest. If a concern is the site of a burglary over and over again, we look upon its owner as a very unlucky man. I believe the Canadian people are really unlucky. It has been like that for three years and it seems that things will not change.
Why not use the reins of power we have to reform the Canadian economy? Why manage in such a way that the taxpayer cannot provide for his most basic needs, by getting out of him the little money that would enable him to live decently?
On the contrary, the Canadian people have to pay absurd taxes like this 3 per cent surtax that the government was to put into force for a year only, a few years ago.
If the government removed the 3 per cent tax, this would encourage the workers, merchants and businessmen, it would help to stimulate the economy which is being jeorpadized by a burden of taxes, surtaxes and temporary taxes of all kinds, the plague of our citizens, especially small wage-earners, industrialists and businessmen.
If the government finally decided to face the truth, and specially to keep the promises made at election time, it would withdraw the bill or at least delay its passing until less drastic solutions are found to restore the Canadian economy. It is high time to do so. It is imperative for the Canadian government to do everything in its power to enable our economy to catch its breath.
To my mind, there are glaring contradictions in the means used by the government in managing our country. When that so-called temporary tax was levied several years ago, it was mainly to control alleged inflation.
Now, on December 3, the government stated that inflation-a term used to conceal the government's mistakes- had been checked. Then, why has that temporary surtax become permanent? Perhaps in anticipation of new inflation or perhaps the government is using that measure to play politics, reserving the right to repeal it before the next election.
After all, as recently stated by the minister, the people who are drawing social welfare or unemployment benefits are wel lpaid by the government. The surtax will increase unemployment still more, because it will take from the Canadian consumers part of their purchasing power which will reach some $245 million for the financial year 1971.
Thus, the government may add that amount to the one already allocated for the support of the unemployed.
Indeed, 25 per cent of the budget is now appropriated for social welfare and 14 per cent for development and economic support.
Mr. Speaker, we are spending more money on people doing nothing than to get the economy back on the road. Thanks to the amount produced by this 3 per cent surtax, the government will find funds to increase unemployment insurance benefits.
Hard as I try, I cannot begin to understand the logic behind this government, which leaves people unemployed, and then assists them through all sorts of social welfare schemes. I want to make this clear: I am not against the principle of social welfare, but against whoever wants to keep people out of work, as this is happening now.
This is nonsense, in such a rich country, and I would surely not want to be in the position of the Minister of Finance who can see numerous debts falling due and finds himself forced to keep a great number of Canadians in poverty, because of the shortcomings of the present system.
As long as the wheels of the Canadian economy have not been changed, Canadians will be forced to keep on pulling this wagon toward a destination which looks rather gloomy.

Mr. Speaker, Bill C-255, which the Minister of Finance (Mr. Benson) is asking us to extend for another year, seems somewhat dishonest to me, since in 1968, the same minister levied a 3 per cent tax which was to have been for a period of one year. The Minister of Finance will be reducing the income of those earning small salaries by some $200 million in purchasing power.
Mr. Speaker, taxes are robbery when applied to taxpayers who do not have enough money to acquire the requisites for a decent life while there is an abundance of products in the country. Taxes are robbery so long as there are unsold products, forced unemployment, unused productive capacities due to lack of sales of products resulting from lack of purchasing power.
Mr. Speaker, taxes are robbery in a period such as the one in which we live, because they reduce purchasing power, result in the overstocking of products and despoil the population just as inflation does.
Mr. Speaker, we of the Ralliement creditiste, are against the extension of the provisions of Bill C-225 for the following reasons: taxes should be intended only to take excess money out of circulation when products are scarce. When there is a shortage of money, the answer is not more taxes but a distribution of the purchasing power by means of a dividend or a compensated discount which would bring prices back to the level of the actual cost of production.
The financing of governments and public investments must be achieved through new financing or new credits according to the actual needs and the production capacity of a country.
To be efficient and socially adequate, an economic system must fulfil two conditions. Firstly, it should be



able to produce goods to meet the needs of the people, and secondly, to distribute those goods in such a way that they meet the needs where they exist.
The Minister of Finance (Mr. Benson), in introducing Bill C-225, goes against the logic of that "just society," about which the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) talked so much during the 1968 election campaign.
At the present time, there is not enough purchasing power to meet the needs of our many workers.
Do we in Canada lack anything necessary to fill the temporal needs of our Canadians, Mr. Speaker? Are we without sufficient food to satisfy the hunger of all? Do we lack shoes and clothing? Are we incapable of producing enough goods to meet the general demand? Do we lack railroads and other means of transportation? Do we lack wood and stone to construct a good house for every family? Are there not enough contractors, carpenters and other types of workers necessary to build them? Is there an insufficiency of machinery? As a matter of fact, we have all these things and more; in fact, we could have a lot more in Canada if our Minister of Finance (Mr. Benson) would only stop taxing the poor.
We have three-quarters of a million people who want to produce for the benefit of those in need, but they are paralyzed by the unfair policy of the Minister of Finance. Mr. Speaker, if there are a great many things to sell in a country, then logically there must be a great deal of money in order that these goods may be purchased. The more people and goods the more money there must be in circulation, otherwise the flow of goods is stopped. Money was created for the purpose of moving products into the hands of consumers. Why, then, does the necessary money not find its way into the hands of the people in amounts equal to the flow of goods from the production line?
The founder of Social Credit, Major Douglas, had this to say, "The industrial system, which makes goods, is not to blame for poverty; it is the financial system." We will never build a strong Canada by taxing those with low income for the benefit of those with high income, Mr. Speaker. This proves to us that the government always protects the strongest in the country
With Bill C-225, our Minister of Finance is attacking not only the individual with an ample income but also the individual with the bare minimum of income. He is taxing what is necessary to life, and that is money. People cannot live without money, even though we have plenty of everything in Canada.
When the Bank Act was passed, the Rothschild brothers, under date of June 25, 1863, wrote as follows:
It (this act) gives the National Bank almost complete control of national finance. The few who understand the system will be either so interested in its profits, or so dependent on its favours, that there will be no opposition from that class...the great body of the people, mentally incapable of comprehending will bear its burden without complaint.

Mr. Speaker, a while ago I noted that some ministers in the House seemed to find the Social Credit opposition
Division
strange. In 1934, the Right Hon. Lyon Mackenzie King, then leader of the opposition had this to say:

Once a nation parts with the control of its currency and credit it matters not who makes the nation's law. Usury, once in control will wreck any nation. Until control of currency and credit is restored to Parliament and recognized as its most sacred responsibility, all talk of sovereignty of Parliament and of democracy is idle and futile.

Mr. Speaker, I believe that the words spoken by the former Prime Minister of Canada are clear enough to convey to the government that this is truly the case at the present time.
There is an abundance of goods, the people want to work, but, because of our financial system, they cannot do so and must rely on welfare to support their families.
I believe, Mr. Speaker, that it is unfair, especially to the workers of Canada, to maintain the 3 per cent tax.

subsubtopic: REQUEST FOR COPY OF CONTRACT FOR SALE OF RESEARCH REACTOR TO TAIWAN
speechtext:
That an humble address be presented to His Excellency praying that he will cause to be laid before this House a copy of the contract between the Atomic Energy of Canada Limited and the Atomic Energy Council of Taiwan regarding the sale of a nuclear research reactor.
He said: Mr. Speaker, on November 4, 1970 I asked that the contract between Atomic Energy of Canada Limited and the Atomic Energy Council of Taiwan regarding the sale of a nuclear research reactor be tabled in this House. The reason I asked that the terms of the contract be tabled is that there is a growing suspicion among many Canadians that we are having difficulty in selling reactors in the export market. This growing suspicion was confirmed in the month of March 1971 by the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Greene), who admitted that Canada's attempt to sell nuclear reactors in the export market has been a dismal failure. The minister went on in no uncertain terms to cite the poor record Canada has in this regard and indicated that efforts to sell nuclear reactors in Finland, Argentina, Yugoslavia, Roumania and now Australia had failed.
I note that some members on the other side of the House look on this matter rather lightly, failing to realize the tremendous loss suffered by Canadians not only in terms of profit but in terms of employment. I am sure that when they have heard my remarks, and the remarks of some of my colleagues, they will take a more serious attitude to this question. We in Canada had high hopes that our CANDU system would make its mark in the sale of nuclear reactors throughout the world, that it would create not only a great deal of employment for Canadians but would produce a profit as well. The minister has stated that Canada stands little chance of beating a British bid to build a $150 million nuclear power plant in Australia. In other words, we have been up to bat five times and have struck out five times. The question there-
Atomic Energy
fore arises whether we are in the right league in this expensive and important field. Perhaps it is a field that is too expensive, one from which Canada should withdraw.
I suggest there is a comparison here with the ill-fated Arrow project. You will recall, Mr. Speaker, that back in 1958 and 1959 Canada launched a program to sell aircraft to other countries. After an expenditure of some $300 million we had to cease production of the ill-fated Arrow, resulting in a great loss of money and, more importantly, loss of employment and potential markets. It was said at the time that the reason for the loss of sales was that many of the major powers that would have been purchasing the ill-fated Arrow had insufficient confidence in the ability of 20 million people to produce such a high powered and high priced aircraft. We now have an analogy in the nuclear reactor field. This is the reason I have brought this matter to the attention of the House, and I am asking that the details of the contract between the Taiwan government and the Canadian government regarding this sale be put before the House so that a study can be made to determine whether we should withdraw from this field.
One is reminded of the glowing optimism displayed by the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources a year ago March when he literally put his cabinet portfolio on the line with regard to the potential of the CANDU system, saying that we stood an excellent chance of penetrating the market, making sales, creating employment and producing profits for Canadian companies. Now, like a dog with its tail between its legs, he is running for cover, trying to cloak himself with excuses. The minister may be right. We may be in a very expensive field in which our research know-how is insufficient to compete with that of the United States and some European countries. As the minister indicated, it looks as though we are going to fail in our bid to sell a $150 million reactor to Australia. However, I would remind the minister of the remarks he made about the CANDU system, which uses natural uranium and heavy water to moderate an atomic reaction and to transfer the heat to the generating turbines. If I am correct-and I must admit to very limited knowledge of this specialized field-this would mean that countries in the world would not have had to depend on our neighbour to the south which is the main supplier of enriched uranium.
It is very easy to have hindsight and to be able to criticize a government that has failed so many times. But, Mr. Speaker, I think you should appreciate that my intention, and the intention of the members of my party, was to draw the attention of the minister and members of the government to the serious situation that prevails. We wanted to know what were the terms of the contract between the Canadian and the Taiwan governments since it would have been foolish for the minister to misrepresent the position of Canada in this very important field.
One is quick to realize the limitations of a country like Taiwan, which is why one becomes rather suspicious that in announcing a sale to Taiwan the government may be attempting to cover up. In fact, this is not a sale in the real sense of competing with other countries in the


Atomic Energy
supply of a nuclear reactor but more an extension of foreign aid to this particular country. It therefore behooves me, as a member of the New Democratic Party, to ask why the government refuses to place the terms of this contract before members so that we may study them. It may be said that the terms are very confidential and that to disclose this information might be detrimental to Canada's position in bidding in this field. I am sure that the members of our party, as well as members of the opposition, are fair and reasonable men and if the minister had said that he would agree to a meeting of the natural resources committee, the meeting could have been held in confidence. Let me point out to you the difficulties we are having in competing in foreign fields. The contract between Taiwan and Canada was more in the nature of foreign aid than the result of high powered competition among countries throughout the world. Had it been otherwise, members of the committee might have been able to report their satisfaction.
I have had great respect and regard for the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources throughout the years. I know he has had legal training and has a legal mind. He has been able at times to persuade Canadians, in a rather shallow and empty way, to accept certain matters. When I look at some of his energy policies, I am acutely aware that we must be alert at all times to make judgments which are objective rather than subjective, completely dependent upon the minister and his officials.
Therefore, I have great confidence that the minister will agree to this motion this afternoon. I am sure he will agree to refer the matter to the appropriate committee and will appear before that committee with his officials to give the details of this contract as well as the problems we are facing regarding the sale of nuclear reactors. I would think if he sets forth the problems he has, and listens to the constructive criticisms of members of the committee, he may be able to salvage something in respect of this very important undertaking. I will not take any more of the time of the House because I have the greatest confidence in the minister. I know he will present his problems so we can study them and be better equipped to suggest solutions.

Historically, Canada's position as one of the five most advanced nations in atomic energy development may be said to have had its origins in the discovery and exploitation of uranium deposits for the production of radium in the 1930's. The switch during the war to interest in uranium for nuclear weapons development, concurrently with the need for a base for the British atomic energy research program, brought Canada into the tripartite council with the UK and the United States. Moreover, French scientists, who had pioneered the idea of the heavy water natural uranium chain reactor, were working with the UK team. Canada undertook, jointly with them, to develop the heavy water reactor for the production of plutonium. Based on pilot experiments with the ZEEP, a zero energy pile which started operating at Chalk River, Ontario, in 1945, the adjacent NRX reactor was built and came into operation in 1947. It was so successful that in 1949-50 both the United States program of giant heavy water production reactors at Savannah River and the combined research and production reactor, NRU, at Chalk River, were committed.
To conduct the growing program of atomic energy research and development involving reactor construction and operation and the production of isotopes, the Crown


Atomic Energy
company, Atomic Energy of Canada Limited, was formed in 1952 to take over the research from the National Research Council and the radioisotope business from a sister Crown company, Eldorado Mining and Refining (1944) Limited.
The direct cost of the NRX reactor did not exceed $10 million. The NRU reactor, completed in 1957, cost $58 million but earned a revenue of more than $30 million from the sale of plutonium to the U.S.A. Since 1951 these two main reactors at Chalk River have also produced radio-cobalt-cobalt-60-and other isotopes for commercial sales and use in cancer therapy units, and in irradiators for sterilizing packaged medical supplies and other purposes.

The Canadian isotope production business has increased from about $500,000 in 1952 to a sales volume of more than $10 million per year. Research and development have grown from prime interest in nuclear physics, chemistry and biology to embrace basic materials research and large-scale engineering for nuclear power.
Canada's development of a distinct line of highly economical nuclear power reactors has now reached the stage of initial commercial acceptance by electric utilities. This has been achieved in spite of the fact that our expenditures for nuclear power development have been very modest compared with those of the U.S.A., U.S.S.R., U.K., France, and now Western Germany and Japan. Much benefit has been derived from technical collaboration with the U.S.A. and U.K. Similar collaboration is being established with France. Since 1955 there has been successful collaboration with India which has led to the operation since 1961, near Bombay, of the CIRUS reactor similar to NRX and to a sequence of Canadian-designed power reactors of 200 megawatt electrical rating now under construction.
The total employment roll of Atomic Energy of Canada Limited has risen from 1,396 at its formation in 1952 to 4,685 in 1970-not a bad employment record in spite of the remarks of the hon. member for Broadview who said more employment should have been brought about by this particular industry. A more extensive history has been published under the title "Canada's Nuclear Story," by Wilfrid Eggleston.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, Canada's position so far as heavy water is concerned would be much better if the Nova Scotia government had hired expertise from the scientific community of Atomic Energy of Canada instead of running off to the U.S. to hire someone else. But today, with Atomic Energy officials looking into the heavy water plant at Glace Bay to see whether it can be repaired or salvaged in any way, I am sure that production of heavy water in Canada is now in far more capable hands.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I wish I had known earlier that this topic was coming up for consideration today because I have some quite definite feelings on it. He suggested that the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Stanfield), when he was Premier of Nova Scotia, made some serious errors in regard to the heavy water plant at Glace Bay. speechtext:
But there is one thing that I think should be mentioned relating to our export sales, to the fact that we do not produce heavy water to accompany any possible sales of plant that we make abroad and to the difficulty we have acquiring enough heavy water for our own use. It is the fact that Atomic Energy of Canada Limited cannot be absolved of all responsibility in regard to the Glace Bay plant. When Atomic Energy signed a contract with the government of Nova Scotia it should have made certain that the production methods at Glace Bay were of a satisfactory nature. To my knowledge this was never thoroughly checked out by Atomic Energy. If it did not do so, why did it sign the contract on behalf of the federal government? This is a point that should be emphasized.
But, Mr. Speaker, all that is in the past. We want to concern ourselves now with the production of atomic energy in Canada and with sales of plant abroad. We would like to know more about sales abroad; this is the purpose of the motion. Are we going to be able to sell more atomic energy plants abroad? I have visited two atomic energy plants in Canada, the Pickering plant where one unit is completed or practically completed, with three more units under construction, and the prototype plant at Gentilly, Quebec. As a result, I cannot help feeling that the government should have got the lead out sooner with regard to new ideas in the scientific field covering new methods of producing atomic energy.
I was impressed with one of the new ideas being used at Gentilly. One of the main criticisms of the CANDU operation is its high capital cost. The plant at Gentilly is reducing considerably its capitals cost in the sense of boiling light water for steam instead of using heavy water. When one considers that heavy water costs $30 per pound you realize this will reduce the plant's costs and it also cuts out the costs of a heater changer. The plant does not have to worry about losing heavy water at $30 per pound, because what does it matter if it loses only a little ordinary light water. I may be speaking without proof that the plant at Gentilly is going to work. But if I were in the market for an atomic energy plant I would hesitate about purchasing an installation such as the one at Pickering. I would look seriously at the prototype plant in Gentilly because I believe it has good possibilities.



It has been said that capital costs involved in the production of atomic energy are too high. I would point out that these days the costs of producing energy in all fields are going up. When costs in these other fields rise, atomic energy will come into its own. Mention was also made of the late C. D. Howe. There are one or two other items I would also like to mention. Just the other day I read that an American experimental group is producing energy from hydrogen. This is a new concept and one which we may use in the future. There is no radioactive waste in connection with this production. If we are to keep up to date in producing atomic energy, I feel we must invest more money in research. I compliment the hon. member for Renfrew North for recognizing this fact, but part of the problem in any scientific project is paying the development costs. If we have only two or three plants, the development costs are high compared with the cost of the plants themselves. If we could sell 10 or 15 plants, obviously the cost would come down. Mr. Speaker, I am very pleased to enter this debate and speak on the motion introduced by the hon. member tor Broadview (Mr. Gilbert). At the outset I would say that I cannot accept the notice of motion as presented, but with other members I appreciate the opportunity to comment on atomic energy, nuclear power and the agreement with the Taiwan government.
In his remarks the hon. member for Broadview mentioned the concern-I believe he said suspicion, but there is concern-about the fact that the Canadian atomic energy program, so eagerly anticipated for different parts of the world, has not as yet met expectations. However, he misquoted the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Greene) and I should like to set this straight for the record. The minister said that the CANDU reactor, based on the use of natural uranium and heavy water, would stand on its own merits against any other atomic energy system-in our own domestic market. Of course, we have many reactors completed or under construction in Canada: the Rolphton reactor, the one at Douglas Point, Pickering One, Pickering Two, Three and Four are projected, the Gentilly reactor and the Bruce reactors One, Two, Three and Four which are projected in the future.
I want to make it quite clear that the minister was very definite in his statement regarding our domestic market. Of course, in the international market many factors can be involved. We are all aware of the recent discovery of uranium ore in Australia. Of course, our government thought that this would assist us in our discussions and anticipations regarding reactors for Australia. Unfortunately, the British nuclear power group has offered to share with Australia its program on the manufacture of uranium.
There is no question that the CANDU reactor's capital cost is higher, but the operating cost and the differential in price between natural and enriched uranium can play an important part in operating expenses for any power reactor. Of course, the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources says that he is not fixed to the CANDU program. In a speech he made, or at his press conference in Japan last December he suggested it was possible that some capital assistance could be obtained from countries of the Pacific rim to develop a plant for the enrichment of uranium in Canada. I think we have to consider all these factors in regard to the potentiality of our role in nuclear energy in the world.
I now wish to make a few general remarks about the Taiwan contract. I think the hon. member for Broadview and other hon. members would be interested to know that the contract for the reactor was signed in September, 1969. It is not a power reactor, but a research reactor.

The total cost of this project in Taiwan is approximately $35 million, the Canadian content of which will be some $28 million. It is a 100 per cent commercial contract, with no lending arrangements or other special financial considerations. Atomic Energy of Canada Limited is the prime contractor. Most of the Canadian content will be provided by Canadian firms in the form of engineering services, fuel and project management. Construction began at the site in 1970 and is going ahead well, and there is every indication that the project will be completed by 1973. I know that hon. members will be interested to know that the Taiwan authorities agreed to accept the application of the safeguard system of the international atomic energy agency to ensure that the reactor is used for peaceful purposes only.
The Taiwan research reactor, as my colleague said, is a development of the NRX reactor that was first started in Chalk River in 1947 and has twice been rebuilt since that time. Capitalizing on and benefiting from the experience with our NRX reactor, the Taiwan research reactor is a highly sophisticated research and development reactor and was selected by the Taiwan Atomic Energy Commission after much careful consideration of the various research reactors available in the world. It is similar to the CIRUS reactor, originally called the Canada/India Reactor, or CIR, at Trombay, near Bombay, India. This reactor, completed in 1961, was based on the NRX design. Its success and contribution to the Indian atomic energy program undoubtedly influenced the Taiwan decision in favour of a Canadian reactor.
Atomic Energy of Canada Limited hopes, and indeed expects, to market its reactor elsewhere. Roumania has shown serious interest in acquiring one of these NRX reactors for its national atomic energy program.



Roumanian interest was sparked by the integrated nuclear program of India, with its heavy water research reactor and a series of heavy water power reactors starting with the two emits in Rajasthan which are modelled on the design of the Canada, Douglas Point, nuclear power reactor.
Other countries interested in natural uranium-fueled power reactors recognize the merits of the NRX reactor and are potential customers. International bidding for large and expensive items of equipment is intense and contenders, for good reason, do not show any more of their cards than is absolutely necessary. When a job has been obtained it is normal for the total price to be divulged and, possibly, the value of some of the components.
