speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, if it will please the committee, and particularly the hon. member, I will do so. In his comments immediately prior to private members' hour he invited discussion of the government's assessment of the efficacy of the measure proposed in clause 1 of this bill. He also remarked during second reading that I had been the only government member to speak on the bill as I had introduced second reading on behalf of my minister.
In reply to the latter point, I suggest to the hon. member that he would not, I am sure, have made that point had his parliamentary duties required him to attend in the House and listen attentively to the entire


Income Tax Act
debate, as I did. Had he done so he would have recognized that except in a couple ol rare instances the debate did not deal specifically with Bill C-225 but, rather, was of a general nature which really continued the six-day budget debate for a further period, three days so far. Government members participated fully in the six-day budget debate. Being no doubt respectful of the rules of this chamber, and being in accord with the government's economic policies in general and those reflected in this bill in particular, they feel no compulsion to join in extending the budget debate beyond the six days that the Standing Orders provide and which the House had completed prior to the introduction of this bill.
I am here ready, willing and able to deal with specific questions regarding this bill, including those that the hon. member alleges were posed during the second reading debate, although if there were many of them they must have escaped me in spite of my attentiveness. The government is confident that the measure proposed in clause 1 will be an effective incentive for the rather specific purpose for which it is designed, namely, the encouragement of capital investment in new manufacturing and processing facilities. This in turn will have a direct, positive effect in terms of increased employment.
Since the measure will apply to capital expenditures made between December 4, 1970, and March 31, 1972, it is not possible to assess the impact of the proposals with precision at this time, and it will not be possible to do so until after the income tax returns of businesses taking advantage of the incentive have been filed for the taxation years ending between December 4 last and March 31, 1972. What is certain is that the direct effect of the 115 per cent capital cost allowance base on the cash flow of qualifying taxpayers constitutes a very real and significant incentive when taken into account with the cost of financing capital expenditures. Its exact value to a given taxpayer will depend on a number of factors, including depreciation class, interest rates, term of borrowing and so on. Inquiries concerning the proposal, as well as announced capital expenditure intentions, confirm the government's assessment of the value of the incentive.
I might say that I took the opportunity during the dinner hour to review the hon. member's speech on second reading on March 3. I found none of the specifics that he alleged earlier today in his speech. There was a specific in the speech of the hon. member for Edmonton West, who was concerned that the 115 per cent base would be available only for prescribed property not previously used for any purpose whatever. That is precisely the intention, to inspire new plant and facilities, and we make no apology for it.
I commend clause 1 to the committee. If the hon. member has any specific questions relevant to the clause I shall be pleased to hear them and to have an opportunity to respond to them.

Mr. Chairman, perhaps the parliamentary secretary could clarify one matter that has puzzled me a little. I refer to the incentive to encourage enterprises to decide to move forward investment decisions; I
presume that is the purpose of the measure. I am a little puzzled as to the appropriateness of this provision by itself, in view of the forecast of business investment for 1972 received by the Economic Council of Canada, which showed quite a dismal expectation for that year. If the effect of this provision is to encourage enterprises to make investments in 1971 and as far as April 1, 1972, which they would otherwise have made in the year 1972, then it looks like a pretty feeble effort in view of the anticipated investments reported to the Economic Council.

speakerposition: Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs
speechtext: They were made before this bill.

Yes, they were. I would be happy to engage in a debate with the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs who, if he is not careful, may become Minister of Finance himself one day. My point is that since the purpose of the measure seems to be to move forward investment decisions, if the investments to be moved forward are very insubstantial in any event then surely the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance ought to present to this committee some more substantial stimulus in view of the very weak expectations reported to to the Economic Council for 1972 through to 1975.

Mr. Chairman, may I simply say that the forecasts of business expenditures have been out in the past, as my hon. friend has seen for himself today. Last year people were saying that it was a terrible year, whereas the increase in capital expenditures in Canada was 8 per cent, much above what was expected by the Dominion Bureau of Statistics. If we are talking about creating jobs now by means of this kind of incentive and one can write off 15 per cent beyond the cost of a particular asset, I suggest this is certainly a great incentive to moving the installation of that asset back into 1971 as compared with, say, 1972 and 1973. I am not at all worried about the economic forecasts in 1972 and 1973.
I think the economy of Canada is moving upwards and I think it will continue to move upward in spite of the great concern the Leader of the Opposition has expressed. He realizes that this is the case; he knows the economy will move upward in 1971 and through 1972. He knows that is why we are including this particular incentive at this time. In the over-all picture it will mean that a lot of assets will be put in place in the fiscal year 1971-72 which would not otherwise be in existence, in that time.
Hear, hear!

Mr. Chairman, this is exactly what we want to do: we want people to move their capital expenditure programs forward in order that we can create jobs as soon as possible without creating inflation. My hon. friend has talked a great deal lately, even during the question period today, about what is and what is not happening. This kind of program represents an incentive



which businessmen really understand. They understand that when they are investing in their assets the most important thing to them is the cash flow, how much they can write off and the amount of capital available to them and when. I maintain this is a very strong incentive in respect of the movement forward of capital expenditures into the current fiscal year instead of putting them off until the fiscal year 1972-73.
I would simply like to say again that I am not worried about what will happen in 1972-73, although I know this is important to my hon. friend because there might be an election about that time. I think the Canadian economy is moving upward. I am sure it will continue to do so. This will create jobs, and we want jobs as fast as we can get them.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: It is not fast enough.

Mr. Chairman, I was not really asking the minister whether he was worried about investment expectations in 1972-73, because it is quite irrelevant whether he is worried. The fact is that the most accurate and most reasonable indication we have had is that investment in 1972-73, on the basis of the present policies of the government, will be poor. I suggest that the minister should try to move forward in another way rather than following this weak method. He ought to be encouraging expansion in the next few years instead of simply attempting to move forward the investments which have been forecast.
I have made many suggestions to the hon. minister, to which he has paid no heed at all, as to what he might do to stimulate economic growth and investment confidence in this country. Whether the minister is worried, and regardless of the forecast he has made, I would be less than honest if I did not take this opportunity to say I have no more confidence in his forecast today than I had in his forecast in 1968. At that time he forecast a surplus, and we ended up with a deficit of about $700 million.

In answer to that, Mr. Chairman, I should like to say that I have no more confidence in the Leader of the Opposition than I had when he went into Deuterium of Canada Limited. I simply say that the economy is moving upward. This bothers the Leader of the Opposition. He has been running all over the country talking about an election in 1971. He has suggested that we have to call an election now because he knows things are going to be good in 1972. He does not want to see the economy move upward: this is because of political reasons and nothing else. I believe that the Canadian economy will move forward and upward. I believe that in the fiscal year 1971-72 we will find a decline in seasonally adjusted unemployment. I am sure we will also find an increase in the gross national product. People outside this country forecast a much greater increase than I forecast in my budget speech in December. We will also find an increase in productivity in Canada.
I can understand how this upsets the Leader of the Opposition. He really has had a very tough time. He wants to upset everybody in Canada by suggesting that we are not doing things for 1971. All the time in the House of
Income Tax Act
Commons he suggests that we should be creating more jobs now. He suggests the Minister of Finance should be worried about creating jobs in 1972-73 but should not be worried about creating jobs at this stage. I suggest that a government which is responsible must be worried about creating jobs now. A responsible government must be concerned about moving forward, as this government is now doing, with a sound economic policy for Canada. Such a government must adopt a policy to increase the number of jobs, increase the gross national product and decrease unemployment in the economy without undue inflation.
Hear, hear!

I should like to reply to the Minister of Finance. I am not surprised that the country is in the state it is now, in view of the way the minister has attempted to twist what I have said into the suggestion that I am concerned only about unemployment in 1971. What I am saying is that the measures being put forth by the minister are inadequate to sufficiently stimulate employment in 1971. His suggestion that I am worried is irrelevant. The fact is that there are about 750,000 unemployed people today as a result of the government's inflationary policy.
I am surprised that the minister would play politics with an issue as important as this. I suggest to him that it is not adequate to provide an incentive designed to move investment forward in 1972-73 to 1971. This is particularly true when the forecast by the Economic Council of Canada is so dismal in respect of these years. What the minister ought to be doing is listening to someone other than himself. He should be attempting to stimulate investment generally, rather than relying on a forward movement in the coming fiscal year. He is thinking in terms of investment which has already proved to be inadequate. Instead of this mockery in which he is engaging he should be stimulating sound investment during 1971-72 and 1973. I am suggesting that his policies are inadequate to create employment in 1971. I have tried to explain to him why his policies are inadequate, but he does not seem to understand.

Mr. Chairman, I am sorry that the Leader of the Opposition has brought politics into this debate. I suppose the place for politics is the House of Commons. I believe that the policies developed by this government are the best possible. I am sure it upsets the Leader of the Opposition that we are overcoming inflation to a large degree. He never really overcame inflation or unemployment in his province. I like to think back on his speeches last year in which he talked about inflation. I recall his colleague, the hon. member for Prince Edward Hastings, standing up and saying that a .5 per cent monthly increase means we will experience a 6 per cent inflation ratio during the year. This is the sort of thing I heard said a year ago. I am sure the Leader of the Opposition is very upset about the successful developments in the economic situation.


Income Tax Act
I am very upset about the unemployment situation.

The hon. member did nothing about the unemployment situation in Nova Scotia when he was Premier. He is responsible tor starting that province in the direction of a serious debt position. That province will And it very difficult to recover from that situation. In spite of his experience with Deuterium of Canada, he stands up now and says that we should stimulate the economy. How to stimulate the economy at this particular time is really a matter of judgment. We have moved through a period in which the economy has bottomed out and started moving upward. We have done much better in this regard than our neighbours to the south. We have had less increase in unemployment. We have had an increase in our gross national product, whereas theirs has declined; and we have had a price performance which is almost twice as good as that of the United States.
I do not know how much the Leader of the Opposition would expect the Canadian economy to achieve. I would say, however, we are looking forward in Canada-and indeed economists throughout the world and those in Canada say we are looking forward-to a basic growth in our economy. The one thing we must worry about, which I consider to be a very serious matter, is that we do not get back onto an inflationary spiral in this country. The economy is moving upward and is doing much better than any other economy in the western world.
Don't give us that.

Mr. Chairman, I challenge the Leader of the Opposition to read the reports by independent economists, including a report in Business Week a couple of weeks ago which said we are miles ahead of what is happening in the United States, to look at what is happening to the Canadian economy and see if he can say we have not moved through this difficult period, a period which really started about 10 years ago when we moved through an expansionary period in Canada, when we got rid of the last Tory government and moved through a very dangerous inflationary period in Canada.

Mr. Chairman, I am not rising to attempt to say whether the Minister of Finance or the Leader of the Opposition has the greatest cause to be worried. I am inclined to agree, as the Leader of the Opposition has indicated, that by the vigour of his rhetoric the Minister of Finance at least sounded a bit worried. I suggest to the minister that we consider the politics-as I understood him to use that word a few minutes ago-of the particular clause which is before us. I was a little amazed at the argument the minister advanced in supporting what he sees as the merits of this provision, because he launched into a rather windy dissertation on the causes of unemployment and what one should do to correct it.
I could have understood it if the minister had stood up in the House and suggested that in his view this capital cost allowance arrangement was designed to increase the long-term efficiency of the industrial machine of Canada by encouraging firms to invest in modernized equipment. This would have made political and economic sense. But if the minister is going to argue that it will help cope with the current unemployment situation and will have the effect of reducing unemployment, I would like him to bring some cold, hard statistics and facts before the committee to bolster and verify his argument.
My own observation is that the immediate result of the introduction of new machinery into plants is a reduction in the level of the work force required in a particular form of production. As a matter of fact, unless the minister can prove otherwise, this is almost axiomatic. There may be a long-term effect in the stimulation of the economy that over a period of time will lead to a total increase in the level of economic activity and which will have a beneficial impact in respect of the numbers of people required in the work force, but that was not the basis of the minister's argument.
The minister was trying to tell the committee that this clause would have an immediate beneficial effect on the unemployment picture. He could argue that there would be more employment in construction, but if he wants the House to give serious consideration to his proposal he should say exactly what he means. He should say how much this will improve employment, and in what sector of the work force, for how long it will improve it and what will be the net result in relation to construction
Income Tax Act
activity as compared with the reduction, if any, that will take place in the production work force.
To give an example of what I have in mind, Mr. Chairman, I remember that we had a discussion on this very point when the President of the Privy Council first made the announcement in the House about the decision to construct the heavy water plant at Glace Bay, Nova Scotia. I asked him questions on this very subject. He had made a statement to the effect that it would be a great stimulation to employment in that area of Nova Scotia. But when some of us tried to pin him down, we discovered that while there might be a very temporary increase in the number of employed, the actual number of permanent jobs to be created by that project would be very small.
Rather than taking off into flights of fancy about what this clause will do in relieving unemployment, it seems to me the Minister of Finance should analyse the effects of his proposal, for the benefit of the committee, in such a way that those of us who are prepared to give it serious consideration on its political and economic merits would have some grounds to go on.

If he wants more proof he can look into the record at a question asked by the then hon. member for Halifax, now the Premier of Nova Scotia, when he stood up in this House of Commons and asked the then Minister of Labour whether he would continue the same type of representations that brought the heavy water plant to Glace Bay. I say the record is quite clear. They claimed credit at that time when it appeared to be a very sound investment, and I still say it is sound.
[Mr. Maclnnis.)
What has happened there is technical. It is a difficulty which I am sure the engineers can correct, given the proper opportunity to do so. But the record shows that it was the then minister of industry, who is now the President of the Treasury Board, and the then Minister of Labour, who is now President of the Privy Council, who claimed credit for this, as well as the premier of the province of Nova Scotia who is on the record as having given full credit to the then Minister of Labour for bringing this plant to Nova Scotia. Furthermore, it is on the record of the House that the then Minister of Labour, who also represents the province of Nova Scotia, took full credit for the fact that there will be 2,000 jobs involved in the construction of this plant.
I am telling the Minister of Finance that this is only part of the story, and if I get into the details of it I will give him a few more shocks. It is within the power of the government to correct the mistake with which they have burdened the Nova Scotia government, whereby the province is in the position of trying to finance something which, as the minister said, is above their means. This they did at the insistence of the federal government of the day. The record is clear. I ask any member on the other side of the House who would like to contradict me to stand up now and tell me that I cannot produce from the records of this House the claims made at that time by the then minister of industry, the then Minister of Labour and the present premier of Nova Scotia. They are all on record as claiming the credit. Now let us see them go ahead and bring about what I want to see in Glace Bay.
The minister need not point the finger any more, because there is a great deal of responsibility over there. The minister might want to refer to the fact that if the plant had not been originally brought into Glace Bay, there is no question that a plant would not have been established in Port Hawkesbury. When it comes to the question of Deuterium of Canada, I could say something about this and thereby tell a tale which the minister would not want recorded in this House. But if he wishes to insist on this point, the minister will do a great disservice, not only to the heavy water industry but to the Atomic Energy Commission of Canada.

Mr. Chairman, some of the exchanges that we have heard tonight between members of the government and members of the official opposition remind me of two schoolboys who start a dialogue that goes something along these lines, "You are a stinker," followed by "You are a stinker too", followed by "You are a bigger stinker", and on and on it goes.
However, I want to thank the parliamentary secretary for providing an answer to one of my questions tonight when he gave the figure of $450 million as being the total benefit which the government estimated would accue to corporations, for the most part as a result of the extension of capital cost allowances between December 4, 1970, and March 31, 1972. He also pointed out that of this sum, $25 million would be written off, it was estimated, during the 1971-72 fiscal year. The minister also pointed out in answer to my question that it was estimated that the revenue increase as a result of the proposals contained in clause 2 to extend the 3 per cent surtax in 1971 would amount to $240 million. The greater proportion of this $240 million will of course be charged against individuals as they pay their individual income tax, and a portion of it will apply to corporations paying corporation income tax. So when we say the sum approaches $200 million, I am not sure what the exact figure is in terms of the ratio between the two taxes. It will approach $200 million which will be charged to individuals as a result of the changes to be effected under this bill.

There will also be a net benefit of $450 million to corporations, less the extra amount that they will have to pay in corporate income tax on the other side of the ledger, as a result of this legislation. Thus we see that we have a transfer of benefits as a result of this legislation, Mr. Chairman. Under the proposals contained in clause 1, corporations and business enterprises of this country will achieve a significant saving; they will benefit a great deal. If it could be safely said that this would stimulate the economy and make it healthier, possibly some justification or rationale could be developed to support the government in the proposals we are now considering.
I noted that the parliamentary secretary in his remarks after 1 had asked him some questions shortly after eight o'clock, indicated that he had reviewed my speech of March 3 during the supper hour. I do not know if he had read it before then. However, he seemed to indicate that he did not find too much to comment on in the speech. If that is his view, he is entitled to it. I ought to point out to him, in case he happened to overlook it, that I referred to the impact and some of the consequences that would flow from some of the proposals in this legislation. I draw his attention to the statement to be found near the bottom of the first column on page 3930 of Hansard of March 3, where I said:
There are really two Important consequences which arise out of this which should be noted. The first is that businessmen could accelerate their investment plans or proceed with investment plans that had previously been marginal, both in order to take advantage of the more generous allowance being proposed. Secondly, businessmen who had already made investment plans will receive a windfall gain.
The proposition that such a change in capital cost allowances as is contained in this clause will benefit enterprises which might be considered marginal does, of course, involve some judgment and might be difficult to support in argument one way or the other. I simply advanced it as a point which should be subject to further study. I do not know whether the government has studied this point or whether it has conducted any studies on the consequences of this proposal. The other suggestion was that businessmen could accelerate their investment plans. This may be so. I want to deal with that point later, Mr. Chairman. That, of course, is another point that I feel deserves consideration and further comment by the government.
The other point I raised was with respect to businessmen whose investment plans had already been made. I suggested that they were going to be the beneficiaries, for the most part, of a windfall gain resulting from this change in capital cost allowances. That, of course, is not just my assertion or suggestion; that proposition has been brought forward by reputable people who have given the matter close study. I noted later in my remarks that I felt the proposals presented by the government with respect to the proposed change in capital cost allowances would not have very much impact in 1971; they would not have very much impact right now-and this is the time, of course, when the economy needs stimulation.

I pointed out that there could be some resulting distortions in terms of benefits received as a result of this change in capital cost allowances. I also pointed out that the DBS survey of capital spending intentions for the 200 largest companies in Canada indicates an 11 per cent increase in 1971. That survey was taken before the Minister of Finance made his budget statement. I pointed out that the increases in the manufacturing sector are expected to be rather moderate. That by itself could be used as justification for some policy change, if it would have a beneficial effect on the economy.
I also pointed out that while the over-all change in capital investment in manufacturing be considered rather moderate in impact, there were considerable differences as between various sectors of manufacturing industries. It was noted that the Economic Council of Canada, in its medium term capital investment survey, projects about a 9 per cent increase in 1971 for all industries and some 6.2 per cent in the manufacturing sector. For foods and beverages there is an increase of only 1.2 per cent; for pulp and paper there is a drop of 11.9 per cent; for primary metals, an increase of 40.8 per cent; for chemicals, an increase of only 11.4 per cent; for transportation equipment, a drop of 36.6 per cent; and for others, an increase of 15.7 per cent.
The primary metals industry, which is to experience a 40 per cent increase in its capital expenditures during 1971 as a result of plans made prior to the budget statement of last December 3, will benefit a great deal as a result of these proposals. The pulp and paper industry on the other hand, which is currently suffering from overcapacity, will not receive very much from these proposals. Thus we see a very uneven impact on the economy as a whole resulting from this proposal.
Later, Mr. Chairman, I also noted that a Financial Post survey published in the December 12, 1970, issue suggests that the immediate reaction of companies surveyed was not one of enthusiasm for the proposal of the Minister of Finance. I drew the attention of the House to part of an article in the Financial Post of that day which reads:
Ottawa's policy makers are counting heavily on the budget's extra write-off to spark new capital investment in 1971-but so far industry is reacting coolly to the incentive.
Finance Department officials told Financial Post they expect that the rise in capital cost allowances to 115 per cent will have the biggest economic impact of the various measures proposed.
Industry-to judge by an FP round-up of opinion this week- thinks the incentive will provide "only minor stimulus" to industrial expansion.
That is the view of most makers of pulp and paper, food equipment, plastics, steel, computers and other products canvassed by FP. Only a few companies said Benson's proposal might have any effect on their expansion plans.
I drew the attention of the House to some of the reasons for this situation as pointed out in this Financial Post article. In that connection I read these paragraphs:
But design, land, purchase, and other preliminary activity would take about a year and a half. Construction could probably only be started when Benson's program was ending.
Ironically, companies that had already made expansion decisions but had not yet received machinery or equipment or


taken possession of new buildings will receive an unexpected windfall.
Thus it seems to me that we must consider a serious problem. If the Minister of Finance and his parliamentary secretary have learned anything as a result of their studies, or as a result of their contacts with business and industry, which would counter the propositions put forward in this article we should like to hear them say so. The House and the committee are entitled to hear them because, Mr. Chairman, we are considering a very generous new capital cost allowance to business and industry. We have to make certain that it will achieve the objective hoped for by the government and that in fact it is introduced in an equitable fashion. I think there is little hope for the latter. That is a question we could argue at considerable length: it is a very important matter.
We still have not heard the government's assessment of the situation with respect to its stated objective of stimulating economic growth in Canada. As I indicated earlier, one of the major points we made on second reading was that this proposal would have very little impact at the present time. It will have very little impact during the life of the proposal. It may encourage or stimulate some further activity. However, Mr. Chairman, I suggest the time for economic stimulus is now. There are 668,000 people out of work. When the latest figure is published shortly it will probably be somewhere in the area of 750,000. Most reputable studies indicate that the pick-up in the economy through most of 1971 will be relatively slow. It will be near the end of 1971 before there is any build-up of economic activity. That will be near the end of the period when the benefits will be available.
In his exchange with the Leader of the Opposition earlier, the Minister of Finance expressed his concern about inflation in the future. I wish we had some evidence that his financial proposals are constructive. The proposals contained in this bill are such that they will contribute to any inflationary trends that may develop during 1972. I suggest that we have a quite different consideration. It has been suggested on a number of occasions that the government is not very concerned about economic activity being stepped up quickly at the present time. The government would like to pace it. In fact, the government would not be at all unhappy to see economic activity really begin to build up near the end of 1971 and continue into 1972. The situation in 1972 would then be as suggested earlier by the Minister of Finance. The reasons for this are not only well known to the Minister of Finance but to all members of this House.
If a different course were adopted and there were a tax cut, an increase in exemptions or a changeover to a tax credit system now, this would be of direct benefit to Canadian taxpayers. It would provide the needed stimulus in the economy at the present time-not six months, nine months or a year from now-when the minister would like to see the highest level of pick-up in our economy. We need stimulus now to deal with the problem of the thousands of people out of work. In his earlier
Income Tax Act
remarks the minister spoke about the success of the policy of the government. I am sure those words sound very hollow to those out of work at the present time.
In my remarks on second reading I pointed out-the parliamentary secretary seems to have overlooked this- some remarks made by the Minister of Finance in an interview with a reporter of the Monetary Times in September, 1968. He pointed out that he had some doubts about the way the capital cost allowance program was working. It has been stated on a number of occasions that the government is going to review the capital cost allowance program and the manner in which it is working. I do not know what stage that review has reached. There are further features built into this program as a result of the proposals of the government. The government is going to use the capital cost allowance program as a further stimulus. They think this will help the economy, while at the same time they have serious doubts about the entire program. This is a matter of real concern.
There are two other concerns which should be noted. One, which I referred to in my remarks of March 3, is in connection with the regional implications of this program. What effect will it have in terms of regional development in Canada? Is there any co-ordination between our regional development programs? There is now a very high level of assistance to many companies in various parts of Canada to expand their secondary manufacturing and processing facilities. This is of very material benefit to many of these companies.
Serious doubts are being cast on this program at the present time. I do not intend to deal with them now. However, it must be noted that there are implications involved in terms of the proposals presented by the government in this legislation. We need to examine what impact this measure will have on the entire regional development program.
I wish to comment on one further point which deserves consideration. That is the question of the relationship of the government' proposals in this clause to its forthcoming policy on foreign ownership. We presume this will be brought forward within a reasonable time. Has there been any attempt to take account of the government's policy in the coming weeks, months or possibly years, if it drags on that long? I presume that this legislation will be of as much benefit to American and other foreign-owned concerns as to Canadian concerns.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order please. I regret to interrupt the hon. member, but his time has expired.

Mr. Chairman, I shall be brief. I have a few questions to ask the Minister of Finance (Mr. Benson).
Why has he forced Canadians into unemployment under the pretext of fighting inflation? If he imposed the 3 per cent tax to control inflation, how come we are told today that inflation has disappeared all of a sudden? Why in the name of economic conditions, is there now a proposal to extend the application of this surtax under


Income Tax Act
the pretence that it will allow investments, reduce unemployment and create incentives?
Could the minister explain what is logical in all this?

I very much respect the opinions of the hon. member for Compton. When the government introduced its budget last December it had to make the very serious decision whether it would stimulate the economy through increasing expenditures in selected areas of Canada where unemployment was very high, or whether it should take general measures with regard to a tax reduction. At that time the government decided it must choose to spend money in selected areas rather than make a general, across the board tax reduction.
I appreciate that one is walking a thin line: how much can a government raise from the public in order to carry out its activities? The change in the government's position over the past two years has been remarkable. Whereas the government in 1969-70 was taking net cash out of the economy, we are moving into a position where this year we shall be putting more than $1,500 million into the economy and the figure will run over $2,000 million in 1971-72.
It is a matter of choice. We cannot have it both ways. If the government is to put substantially more into the economy by spending in particular areas, tax levels must continue along the same lines, unless it can both reduce taxes and increase expenditures without causing interest rates to rise or pressure on the dollar to increase.

I wish to put a question to the Minister of Finance having to do with the application of this proposal. It has been suggested that it would be of greater benefit to the Canadian economy if some way could be found whereby the benefits proposed in this clause could be restricted to machinery, equipment and facilities which were manufactured in Canada.
I recognize that this might be of benefit to certain Canadian firms, enabling them to raise their prices in an unnatural way. At the same time, there would be undoubted advantages. I wonder whether the minister gave any thought to means whereby this proposal could be restricted to facilities and equipment made in Canada so as to ensure that the greatest benefit from this proposal, to the extent that there may be any benefit, would accrue to Canada and Canadians.

Certainly the government is interested in having as much of the equipment manufactured in Canada as possible. However, we did not think this particular provision in the Income Tax Act should be limited in the way suggested. After all, we are trying to encourage investment of all kinds. As far as the encouragement of the manufacture of machinery in Canada is concerned, tariff barriers are set so as to discourage the entry of foreign equipment. Only in cases where people can prove, through the machinery adjustment board, that the machinery they require is not manufactured in Canada may they import machinery at favourable rates. The object
[Mr. Latulippe.l
the hon. member seeks is handled through other means than the measures we are introducing here.

Has the minister any estimate as to the proportion of machinery and equipment which is likely to be Canadian in origin, or principally Canadian in origin, as a result of expansion carried out in consequence of these arrangements?

That is a difficult question to answer because the proportion varies so widely as between industries. Other programs approved by the House tend to encourage the manufacture of machinery in Canada as far as possible. I recently had dealings with spokesmen for a particular industry who wished to take advantage of this program, and I emphasized the importance we place upon having machinery manufactured in Canada if at all possible. In connection with several major projects now under way, the people concerned have tried very hard to have the machinery manufactured in Canada as far as possible, and the Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce, together with my own department, have given every encouragement to work in this area.

The legislation now before us deals with the subject of assistance to industry generally. It would be interesting to know whether the minister has given any consideration to the situation of those who have to travel to their places of employment and pay for the tools they use. I realize this may not be relevant to the bill before us but having regard to the assistance this measure is designed to bring to those engaged in industry, surely action could be taken amending the Income Tax Act so as to make the necessary provision in the two areas to which I have referred.

I can assure the hon. member that in the government's consideration of taxation generally, great consideration is being given to both the points he has raised. They are not involved, of course, in the bill before us, but I can assure him that serious consideration is being given to both those points.

Really! You and I have had enough discussion for one night. With the encouragement of the


opposition, the ceiilng was taken off. There is a bottom level, though.

We remember the famous surtax which at that time was 5 per cent instead of 3 per cent. The government was brought to defeat on that issue, though it would not resign. I understand that because of the shakiness of the dollar at the time there was some question whether the constitutional issue should be pressed. The story has been partly told. Our memories are not so short that we do not recall that occasion.
It seems to me, from what the leading economists both in Canada and the United States are saying, that the only way in which to get the economy rolling, to use the minister's words, is to cut taxes. The minister leaves the impression that this budget does not increase taxes. Nevertheless, the government is reinstating the 3 per cent surtax, thus adding to the incidence of taxation on an individual or on a corporation. So really we are running contrary to everything recommended by economists both here and in the United States. The United States has recommended and has cut taxes. I did not speak on the first clause because enough was probably said, both relevant and irrelevant. But there is nothing in the budget to suggest any stimulation as far as the economy is concerned.
I agree with my leader that this Minister of Finance is unique in his predictions. Every prediction that he has ever made in any budget speech since he has been Minister of Finance, and I have been here all the time he has been Minister of Finance, has been millions and millions of dollars out, so it is difficult to take anything he says seriously. He seems to talk without reference to any authority, economic or otherwise, and as far as I am concerned we cannot take seriously any predictions that he makes tonight or on any other occasion.
Mr. Chairman, may I say we have a mutual admiration society. I believe the same thing of my hon. friend.

Well, I know my words have gone very deep, because he has been very hurt since I attacked him on his white paper. He was a professor at university, and on that occasion I called him a small town bookkeeper. My diagnosis at that time has not really changed as far as his ability as Minister of Finance is concerned. The minister talks of getting the economy rolling. One of the reasons taxes should have been cut is that at the end of this month 300,000 students come out of universities and colleges and enter the market seeking employment.
And there is no plan.

No plan whatever. We have continually asked questions about this and been told that there is a plan up the government's sleeve. Two or three days after the questions were put to the minister and to the Prime Minister we read in the paper that so many million dollars would be provided to enable students to travel either in Canada or overseas. This is a good time, when
Income Tax Act
considering this amendment, to hear from the minister. The minister talks of doing something to get the economy rolling, to provide more jobs so unemployment will drop, so I suggest we should have some definite proposal now, not only for university students but for college students.
I would have thought the minister would have reduced taxes instead of increasing them. I suggest he come forward with an incentive plan for individual business people and corporations whereby if they hire a student they will get a tax benefit as an incentive. Perhaps the government might go in on a 50-50 basis. We do not want to go through another season like last year when thousands of students wandered aimlessly across Canada. Even the students themselves were not impressed with the armouries and other federal buildings that were used as hostels for Canadian youth. The minister said we are doing more for our youth than any other western country, but we are doing less, because there are more university graduates with degrees out of work at the present time than ever before.
I am glad the hon. member for Calgary South is here, because he is a lawyer and knows about this. Indeed, he and the Minister of Finance applauded the government when they had a capital cost deal to kill off the economies of Calgary, Edmonton and Vancouver. Let me inform hon. gentlemen that out of 61 young lawyers graduating in Alberta, 32 students do not have a place to article this year. That is an example of what is going on across this country as far as our youth are concerned.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, on a point of order, I think if the hon. member re-reads the letter he will find that the figure is 81 rather than 61.

Then if that is right, it makes it worse. If my memory serves me right it is 61, but if the hon. member is correct and it is 81, that means there are still 31 or 32 students looking for jobs. Whether it be this field or any other field, what have you got? You have no opportunity, no incentive for youth. This clause should be opposed vigorously because it does absolutely the opposite to creating incentives for business to hire young people and students. The government talks about seasonally adjusted figures, but unemployment is nevertheless on the climb at the present time. I should like the Minister of Finance to prove that the proposition that the only way to increase employment at the present time is to cut taxes is economically unsound. Yet he is increasing taxes and therefore aggravating the situation.
The Minister of Finance attacked our leader and other members of this party. Let me say before the Dress tonight-
What press?
Oh, oh!

Well, the fact there is no member of the press present does not disturb me at all. If the friends of the Minister of Finance agree that the proposed increase in taxes will provide opportunity and jobs for the young people of Canada, they are in the same camp


Income Tax Act
as the Minister of Finance. I should like to hear the minister say now that the fact he is increasing taxes in the budget will get the economy rolling and give opportunity and jobs to Canadians, the young and others. I need not say any more.
Hurrah!

My hon. friends over there, particularly my friend from the Northwest Territories, seem to have got somewhat exuberant over the supper hour, though I do not know why. Perhaps they are more impressed with their supper than with the budget, which is why they are applauding at the present time.
We would not have the nerve to disgrace ourselves like this in the House.

Well, I leave it to the Chairman and to
others to decide who are disgracing themselves now. I see the minister moving back from his squad, the group that has been yelling and shouting all night, which shows that even he is ashamed. I hope the minister will answer my question before others speak. Does he take the position that he is going to give opportunity and jobs to Canadians by increasing the taxes of Canadians? Or, putting it the opposite, more positive way, does he admit that the only real solution, one put forward by people who have knowledge of economics, is to cut taxes and get the economy rolling?
Mr. Chairman, the question asked by my hon. friend I answered in some detail a few minutes ago-
Say yes or no.
-when replying to the question raised by the hon. member for Compton. If my hon. friend reads what I said, he will find I answered this question in some detail.

Mr. Chairman, taking a look at the wording of this clause, it becomes more interesting each year. It, provides:
This section is applicable to taxation years commencing or ending in or coinciding with 1968, 1969, 1970-
And now the government is adding "or 1971". How many more years is this tax going to continue? Our only hope is that we are likely to have an election in 1972 and quite possibly the government might not want to see this tax continued into what presumably will be an election year. I hear some hon. members suggesting it may possibly be 1971, so I guess we are getting to the season for election rumours.
There are some important points to be made in respect of clause 2. I noted statements made by the Minister of Finance when he presented his budget on December 3, and later when he and his parliamentary secretary put forward the reason for continuing this surtax into 1971. At that time they said it was for the purpose of obtaining revenue in view of the government's cash requirements.
Let us compare that with the statement made in 1969 when the minister presented his budget. At that time he said he wanted to make it clear that he was not proposing an extension of this tax from 1969 to 1970 for revenue or cash purposes but for purposes of economic stabilization.
At one time the government extends this tax for purposes of economic stabilization, and by the time it gets around to putting legislation before the House there is a downward trend in the Canadian economy or we find there is a low ebb and the government then suggests it needs more revenue. Consequently, it is going to impose this tax on the Canadian people in 1971. I think we have to go back to the situation which existed on budget night. At that time the Canadian people expected a tax cut or some benefit. The psychological impact of the budget that night was akin to a wet dishcloth in the face. The budget of December 3 last served no good purpose as far as the Canadian people are concerned; in fact, it did a disservice to the Canadian people.
I should like to make it clear that we in this party have suggested on many occasions that there should be an increase in exemptions or, better still, a changeover in respect of the tax credit system. I believe Canadians had a right to expect a tax cut last December. It would have been an effective stimulus to the Canadian economy. It would have had an immediate effect. It would have been beneficial. Instead, we have had a repetition of a tenuous struggle as manifested in the provision contained in clause 1 of this bill.
I suggest the government did not follow the course of tax reduction when it presented the most recent budget because it had an election timetable in mind. The government had taken into account the fact that if it stimulated the economy too soon, this would have an important effect on the economy and a resulting effect on the impending election. As a result, the government decided to take protective measures in respect of the economy, keeping in mind an election in 1972.
The government would never consider anything that involved a reduction in taxes or, for that matter, a tax increase until the time was ripe. I suggest this is the very callous reasoning of the government which led it to bring forward this type of proposal. The government has in mind a time period in respect of tax benefits. Anything that is of benefit to the Canadian economy should be a matter of importance to the government. The Minister of Finance and the parliamentary secretary have made no attempt to come forward with any point to indicate that clause 1 will be of assistance in stimulating the Canadian economy. On the other hand, we have in clause 2 a measure which will dampen the Canadian economy and hold back economic growth.
I suggest this measure will lead to a continuation of high unemployment. I suggest the government will maintain and continue this situation until the time is ripe to stimulate the Canadian economy in preparation for the next federal election.

maintopic: AGRICULTURE-ALLEGED TRAFFICKING IN INDUSTRIAL MILK QUOTAS-REQUEST FOR INFORMATION
AGRICULTURE-ALLEGED TRAFFICKING IN INDUSTRIAL MILK QUOTAS-REQUEST FOR INFORMATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the inquiry I wish to make concerns the matter of trafficking in industrial milk quotas. I think perhaps I should make clear exactly what I mean. Mr. A has a herd of cows and wishes to sell them to Mr. B, who happens to have a sales arena. As a rule, Mr. A also transfers his industrial milk quota to Mr. B. Incidentally, there would seem to be quite a few Mr. B's in the province of Ontario, and no doubt elsewhere. Then Mr. B, who has a sales arena, sells off the herd cow by cow to individuals throughout the country.
Mr. B. then has a quota and he sells the quota to a person in another part of the country, which in most cases seems to be in province of Quebec. The quota is sold to someone who has a herd and not a large enough quota on which to make money. I have received a great deal of information in this regard. I have the names and addresses of a good many vendors, a good many Mr. B's, the intermediary who sells off the herd cow by cow and transfers the quota to somebody else. I do not intend to put the names and addresses on the record because I do not think it would be fair. It is not the fault of the individual but, rather, of the Dairy Commission and ultimately the government for allowing this kind of thing to go on.
One farmer who had a 9,000 pound butterfat quota sold it for $4600 in another province. This kind of trafficking goes on all the time. While apparently this is within the letter of the law, the government and the Dairy Commission have the power to stop it because, as I understand it, the Dairy Commission can prohibit the transfer of quotas either in whole or in part. This, however, is not done. I have more information in front of me, but again I do not wish to place the names and addresses on the record. However, I have substantial information and am prepared to show it to the minister privately.
These traffickers, as I choose to call them, go around to farmers' meetings and tell them they have so many quotas for sale and ask how much they will pay. The fact


Proceedings on Adjournment Motion is the vendor does not do very well. The purchaser of the herd, because the herd is usually bought cow by cow, does not do very well. But the middleman, as in most cases in our country, does very well; he just needs two or three of these transactions in a year in order to do pretty well.
When one has private information in respect of individual cases, one then would like to know the extent to which this kind of trafficking is going on. Therefore I placed a question on the Order Paper-I shall not go into all the details-asking in effect for the number of transactions that took place in Ontario only between April 1 and December 1 of last year. There could not have been too many transactions.

The Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Pepin) did not take that position. We have this situation, and what annoys members on this side of the House is that when something is brought to the minister's attention, instead of looking into it and trying to co-operate he digs in his heels and says no, it is not so. The minister has been in this House for a long time. When he was a member of the Social Credit Party he was critical of government policy, and yet he will not look into these things.

maintopic: YOUTH-CANCELLATION OF CONFERENCE SPONSORED BY CANADIAN COUNCIL ON SOCIAL DEVELOPMENT
YOUTH-CANCELLATION OF CONFERENCE SPONSORED BY CANADIAN COUNCIL ON SOCIAL DEVELOPMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on March 5, I put a question to the Acting Prime Minister regarding the announcement that a conference concerning transient youth and student summer employment had been cancelled. This conference was scheduled for March 14, 15 and 16. I asked the minister why at such a late date the unexpected announcement of cancellation was made. The reply that I received was that the government had been consulting the provinces about a program for student employment and it seemed to them the conference that was to be held might have been useful, but according to the Acting Prime Minister the taxpayers' money could be spent in a more useful way.
What prompted me to ask this question was a communique issued by the Canadian Council on Social Development. I think the best thing to do would be to read the pertinent part of that press release as follows:
The Canadian Council on Social Development announces the cancellation of its conference on Services to Transient Youth and Student Summer Employment scheduled for Ottawa on March 14, 15 and 16. In light of the crisis situation, the council reached this conclusion with deep regret but felt there was no alternative when it was informed by the Department of the Secretary of State that the federal government would neither assist financially nor actively participate. The dates had already been postponed from February 21 to 23 to accommodate federal planning.


Proceedings on Adjournment Motion
The Canadian Council on Social Development which was organizing this conference did not know why the conference had been cancelled. As I have already said, the conference was already scheduled for a period of time in February and because of the federal government it was postponed until March. This suggests to me that someone in the Department of the Secretary of State, one of the officials or perhaps the minister himself, must have given the green light to the organizers of this conference and someone in the department or in the government must have asked the Canadian Council on Social Development to postpone the conference from February until March.
My understanding is that after all the planning had gone into the organizing of this conference, and after many people had become really enthused about the prospects of such a conference which would bring together young people from all across the country-from perhaps 50 or 60 universities-as well as representatives of different community organizations, it was cancelled without explanation a few days before the conference was supposed to take place.
That is why I elected to raise the matter in the "late show" tonight. Hopefully, the congenial parliamentary secretary will shed some light on why that action was taken. The conference, in my opinion, would have been most valuable. It would have brought young people together to discuss what they want to do and means and methods of solving the problems that they have in common. I understand that the federal government would have had to pay only a very small sum in helping to cover the travelling costs of some young people and students who could not afford to bear the expense of coming to Ottawa, the location of the conference.
This conference would have dealt with problems facing transient youth in Canada and suggested suitable programs for them. It would have dealt with the problem of student unemployment and with unemployment among youth in general. In Canada about 45 per cent of our unemployed, I believe, are under the age of 25. This is a very serious problem and we ought to do something about it.
I think that a conference of this sort would have been a small step to providing some of the participatory democracy that our Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) talked so much about two and a half or three years ago. This input by young people would have been valuable because it would have given them more faith in our parliamentary system and government. When you cancel such a conference you are not restoring their faith. You are not restoring hope in the minds of young people about the kind of society we live in or about our government. I am afraid that when things like this keep happening young people will say: You do not look on us as people. You consider us as mere bodies, numbers, small slots in a machine. You do not think we are really here. That is the type of thinking we may find among our young people.
Perhaps the federal government or the department were afraid of any criticism that might have emerged from a conference of young people. I hope the parliamentary secretary can clarify this situation. I suspect that one reason the conference was cancelled was that the government was afraid that young people would be critical of the Prime Minister or of the type of society that this government appears to want. I ask: Why was the conference cancelled at such a late date after the green light had been given? Why suddenly, after all the plans had been made, was the conference cancelled? Perhaps the parliamentary secretary, in the short time allotted to him, will tell us if there are any alternatives open to the young people at this time.

speakeroldname: Mr. James Hugh Faulkner (Parliamentary Secretary to Secretary of State):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State of Canada
maintopic: YOUTH-CANCELLATION OF CONFERENCE SPONSORED BY CANADIAN COUNCIL ON SOCIAL DEVELOPMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the main goal of the Conference on Services to Transient Youth and Student Summer Employment was to urge the government to implement their program in a particular way, and it is at present in the process of achieving that goal. The federal government will be able to make a general announcement on the matter of services to transient youth and summer employment when all consultations with the provinces are completed, which should be some time next week.
As has been said before, the federal government did not feel it would be helpful to participate in a conference prior to the completion of the consultations with provincial ministers and officials, or prior to the formulation of firm proposals for student summer employment. As well, the federal government did not regard such a conference as an urgent need since up to now it has supported a number of similar meetings with public funds. The information accumulated through earlier conferences, in addition to the experience of last summer's programs, was sufficient for the establishment of its new policy, and the consultation process now begun will offer a basis for achieving the main objectives sought by this proposal.
